title: Software Configuration
summary: Software configuration as a mitigation is the deliberate hardening of applications, operating systems, and cloud services away from their permissive defaults, followed by the work of keeping that hardened state true over time. It covers disabling features that exist mainly as attack surface, such as legacy file-sharing dialects, name-resolution fallbacks that answer broadcast queries, obsolete scripting engines, and macro execution from internet-sourced documents; constraining command interpreters with logging and restricted language modes; requiring elevation through a separate administrative account for management tooling; and configuring services so that authentication, transport security, cipher suites, and audit settings match a defined baseline. In cloud estates the same idea appears as account-level and resource-level settings, public-access blocks, instance metadata hardening, and organisation policies that stop a workload owner from reverting a control by accident. The operational reality is drift. Baselines are applied at build time and then eroded by an application that needs an exception, an upgrade that resets a value, a container image that still ships the old configuration, or an operator under pressure who weakens a control to restore service. Teams that succeed treat baselines as code, scan continuously against them, alert on drift, and route exceptions through a named owner with an expiry date instead of leaving them undocumented. The control weakens defence-impairment attempts directly, because central logging configuration and tamper-protected agents remove the easiest routes to silencing telemetry, and it closes the autostart, macro execution, and script-interpreter behaviours that commodity intrusions depend on. Its limits are practical: an exception-heavy baseline is theatre, hardening that breaks operations gets rolled back, and no organisation controls the configuration of every third-party service it relies on.
objectives: Explain how a hardening baseline is derived, applied, and verified rather than assumed to be in place.
Identify default features and services that should be disabled or constrained, and the business justification each removal requires.
Detect configuration drift across endpoints, servers, container images, and cloud accounts using continuous scanning.
Assess how defence-impairment techniques exploit permissive logging and agent configuration.
Design an exception process with ownership, compensating controls, and expiry so that hardening stays credible.
Interpret the tradeoff between tightening configuration and preserving availability for legacy applications.
